turn_text: Let me circle back to where we started in 2010, 14 years later is you prepare to pack up the boxes and head back home. What are you proudest of? What went well over the last seven terms?

Well, I'm going to focus on a few healthcare related things. I've done all kinds of things in transportation and I was part of changing the no child left behind. behind law and education to a better, more palatable system when I was on those committees. But, you know, one of the big things we did in 2015 is we got rid of what's called the sustainable growth rate calculation on how to reimburse providers in Medicare. Replace that with the Medicare and CHIP Reauthorization Act or MACRA, which is better. It's not perfect, but it's better. That needs some further reform. I'm proud of that. Otherwise, we had massive projected cuts every year. We still are having lower cuts and we had some stabilization for a period of time after MACRA. I helped establish what's called Kidney X. Kidney X is a federal prize for innovation in the kidney space where people who are on dialysis to try to get technological innovation to change how we manage long-term kidney care. It hasn't really changed in 50 years. So myself and one of my Democrat colleagues were instrumental in getting the kidney X prize into law. We recently did surprise medical billing where patients who had seen physicians who were accidentally out of their network, unbeknownst to them, were getting these huge bills, right? And the providers weren't getting paid either because insurance plans, wouldn't pay because it was out of network. Surprise medical billing law has fixed that. It's been implemented poorly, unfortunately. But the congressional intent was to be balanced where the providers would get paid a fair market value for their service and the bill wouldn't be handed over to people who were unsuspectively treated by out-of-network physicians. And the last one I'll mention is something we did recently called the Securing US Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network Act. Sounds like a big, big word. It's going to reform the organ transplant network so that we don't have one contract, UNOS, the United Organ Sharing. And we're going to be able to have multiple competitors in the space that we haven't had for the last 40 years. Why do that? We're wasting 20,000 kidneys a year because they should have been properly allocated. The system is overly complex. Transplant surgeons will tell you. This law is going to reform that substantially.
